summary: Catalogs a number of known problems found in TCP implementations. It is informational and was written to help implementers spot and fix common mistakes.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a list of common mistakes people made when building the part of a computer that delivers messages reliably, so builders can avoid them.

subtitle: A catalog of bugs found in TCP implementations and how to fix them.

tldr.problem: TCP implementations commonly have bugs that cause performance issues, connection failures, and unnecessary network congestion. These bugs range from incorrect congestion control to malformed shutdown sequences.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC documents 18 known implementation problems in detail, explaining each bug's cause, how to detect it, and how to fix it. Problems are organized by category including congestion control, reliability, and resource management.
tldr.outcome: This informational document helps implementers identify and correct these problems in their TCP stacks, improving overall network stability and performance.

facts.value: Congestion control, Performance, Reliability, Resource management

today: RFC 2525 is informational and has not been obsoleted. It remains a useful reference for TCP implementers identifying and fixing bugs in their stacks, though many of the issues documented may have been resolved in modern implementations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2525 catalogs 18 known problems found in real TCP implementations. The goal is to improve network stability and performance by making implementers aware of these bugs and their solutions. The problems range from incorrect handling of the congestion window during startup to improper management of connection teardown.

Each problem is documented with its classification, a description of the issue, when it matters, what makes it problematic, relevant specifications, examples from packet traces showing both buggy and correct behavior, and specific guidance on detection and repair. The categories of problems include congestion control, performance, reliability, and resource management issues.
sections.plainLanguage: A list of mistakes people made when writing the code that delivers messages on the internet, so builders can avoid the same mistakes.

sections.title: Congestion Control and Window Management
sections.content:
Several bugs affect how TCP manages its congestion window, the limit on how much data to send before waiting for acknowledgment. The No initial slow start bug causes TCP to send too much data at connection start instead of beginning conservatively and increasing gradually. No slow start after retransmission timeout fails to reset the window when packets are lost due to timeout.

Uninitialized CWND occurs when the congestion window is not properly set during handshake, often due to a missing maximum segment size option. These three bugs can cause traffic bursts that stress networks and trigger cascading packet loss.

The Extra additive constant in congestion avoidance bug adds an extra term (typically MSS/8) when increasing the window, causing the sender to probe more aggressively than the RFC specifies. This leads to multiple packet losses where a single loss would normally occur, and can severely degrade performance without explicit packet loss feedback.

Initial RTO too low initializes the retransmission timeout to a value smaller than the actual round-trip time, causing unnecessary retransmissions and repeated entry into slow start. Failure of window deflation after loss recovery means the congestion window does not shrink appropriately after loss, allowing too much data into the network immediately after recovery.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP is like filling a glass from a pitcher: start slow, increase gradually, and slow down again if it spills. These bugs involve getting those steps wrong, causing overflows or wasted time waiting.

sections.title: Retransmission and Timeout Handling
sections.content:
Several bugs affect how TCP handles lost packets and the timers that detect them. Failure to back off retransmission timeout fails to exponentially increase the timeout between retransmission attempts when packets keep being lost, leading to rapid fire retransmissions that overwhelm congested networks. The RFC specifies that timeouts should double with each retry; failing this causes connections to give up too quickly or to hammer the network excessively.

Retransmission sends multiple packets occurs when a TCP retransmits more than one packet in response to loss. This often happens when TCP options (such as timestamps) are not properly accounted for in the size calculation, causing the implementation to pack too much data into the retransmit, which then gets split into an extra small packet containing data that need not have been resent.

Initial RTO too low (also discussed above) results in retransmissions before the acknowledgment can possibly arrive, starting the cycle of unnecessary retries.
sections.plainLanguage: When a message doesn't get through, we wait a bit, then wait longer next time. These bugs either wait too little or send too many things at once when retrying.

sections.title: Data Delivery and Window Issues
sections.content:
Inconsistent retransmission is a critical bug in which a sending TCP retransmits different data for the same sequence number than it originally sent. This violates TCP's fundamental promise of reliable delivery and can result in the receiver reconstructing a corrupted byte stream.

Failure to retain above-sequence data means the receiver does not buffer packets that arrive out of order (ahead of the next expected byte). When packets are lost and the sender retransmits, a correct receiver should already have the later packets and acknowledge them all at once, allowing the sender to skip over and never retransmit them. Implementations that discard above-sequence data force unnecessary retransmissions of packets that already arrived safely.

Stretch ACK violation occurs when the receiver delays acknowledgments too long or acknowledges more than two full segments worth of data at a time, contrary to RFC recommendations. This causes the sender to transmit in larger bursts, which can overwhelm congested networks. It also slows down the slow start algorithm's window increase since the window grows by one segment per ACK.
sections.plainLanguage: These bugs are about getting messages right: sending the same data twice but with different contents, throwing away messages that arrived but are out of order, or waiting too long to say 'got it', which confuses the sender.

sections.title: Connection Setup, Maintenance, and Teardown
sections.content:
Several bugs affect how TCP manages the lifecycle of a connection. Excessively short keepalive connection timeout closes connections too quickly when no data arrives, requiring only 5 seconds of unacknowledged keepalive probes before giving up. RFC 1122 does not mandate keepalive but requires that if implemented, timeouts allow sufficient time for network recovery.

Insufficient interval between keepalives sends keepalive probes more frequently than the required 2-hour default, wasting bandwidth and risking unnecessary connection termination.

Window probe deadlock occurs in a rare scenario where the receiver's window becomes zero, the sender probes with one byte, and a sign-handling bug in the receiver causes it to compute a negative window and reject all further packets, including acknowledgments of the sender's own data, deadlocking the connection.

Failure to send FIN notification promptly delays the closing handshake by waiting for unacknowledged data to be confirmed before sending the FIN flag, reducing throughput for short-lived connections.

Failure to send a RST after Half Duplex Close does not close the connection when data arrives after the application closes, leading to resource exhaustion as servers accumulate hung connections. Failure to RST on close with data pending is related; it does not immediately close when shutdown is called while data is still queued.

Options missing from TCP MSS calculation fails to account for TCP option headers when calculating the maximum segment size, leading to packets that exceed the link MTU.
sections.plainLanguage: These bugs are about starting, keeping, and ending conversations correctly: hanging up too quickly, checking on someone too often, getting stuck in a bad state, taking too long to say goodbye, or not closing properly when something goes wrong.
